## Task groups and affordability

```{python}
#| include: false

# task-group coefficients from the panel regression (log target), with clustered SEs
panel_coefs = model_log.params[exposure_cols_model]
panel_se = model_log.bse[exposure_cols_model]
mean_afford = model_df["affordability_salary"].mean()

# log coefficient -> % change per 1 percentage point shift -> dollar amount at panel mean
panel_pct_per_point = (np.exp(panel_coefs / 100) - 1) * 100
panel_dollar_per_point = (panel_pct_per_point / 100) * mean_afford

panel_se_pct_per_point = (np.exp(panel_se / 100) - 1) * 100
panel_dollar_se_per_point = (panel_se_pct_per_point / 100) * mean_afford

panel_effects = pd.DataFrame({
    "dollar_per_point": panel_dollar_per_point,
    "dollar_se_per_point": panel_dollar_se_per_point,
}).rename(index=label_map)

largest_group = panel_effects["dollar_per_point"].idxmin()
largest_group_dollar = abs(panel_effects.loc[largest_group, "dollar_per_point"])
largest_group_se = panel_effects.loc[largest_group, "dollar_se_per_point"]
```

```{python}
#| include: false
exposure_ranges = model_df[exposure_cols_model].agg(["min", "max", "mean", "std"])
coefs_per_point = ols_model.params[core_features] / 100  # per 1-percentage-point

effects = {}
for col in exposure_cols_model:
    low = exposure_ranges.loc["mean", col] - exposure_ranges.loc["std", col]
    high = exposure_ranges.loc["mean", col] + exposure_ranges.loc["std", col]
    range_pts = (high - low) * 100
    effects[col] = coefs_per_point[col] * range_pts

effects_series = pd.Series(effects).rename(label_map).sort_values() # this is for std bar chart if we want
```

The panel regression returns a negative association between routine intensive work and
affordability salary that holds after controls. A one percentage point shift toward
`{python} largest_group` work is associated with roughly
\$`{python} f"{largest_group_dollar:,.0f}"` (± \$`{python} f"{largest_group_se:,.0f}"`)
less in affordability salary, evaluated at the panel mean.

@fig-coefplot shows each task group's coefficient with its confidence interval, non
routine cognitive as the reference.

<!-- FIGURE: fig-coefplot. NEW, poster has it as an In Progress placeholder only.
     Coefficient plot, task group on the y axis, association with affordability salary on
     the x axis, points with error bars, non routine cognitive as the reference. The
     figure that turns the whole project into one number, so it carries more weight than
     any other here. -->

```{python}
#| label: fig-coefplot
#| fig-cap: "Task group association with affordability salary (log target), non-routine cognitive as reference. Points show coefficients; bars show 95% confidence intervals from county-clustered standard errors."

coefs = model_log.params[exposure_cols_model]
ci = model_log.conf_int().loc[exposure_cols_model]
errors = [(coefs - ci[0]).values, (ci[1] - coefs).values]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.errorbar(coefs.rename(label_map), coefs.values, yerr=errors, fmt="o", capsize=5, color="#4C72B0")
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1, linestyle="--")
ax.set_ylabel("Coefficient (log affordability salary)")
ax.set_title("Task group coefficients vs. non-routine cognitive")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The associations survive the addition of poverty rate and the other baseline controls, so
the task groups are not standing in for poverty. @fig-coefcompare puts the coefficients
before and after controls side by side.

<!-- FIGURE: fig-coefcompare. NEW, poster has it as an In Progress placeholder only.
     Paired coefficient plot or forest plot, each task group before and after adding
     poverty and the baseline controls. Answers the objection that the task groups are
     poverty in disguise, which the importance chart invites. -->

```{python}
#| label: fig-coefcompare
#| fig-cap: "Task group coefficients before (baseline) and after (full model) adding poverty and demographic controls. Stable coefficients indicate task groups are not standing in for poverty."

baseline_coefs = ols_model_base.params[exposure_cols_model]
full_coefs = ols_model_log.params[exposure_cols_model]

x = np.arange(len(exposure_cols_model))
width = 0.35

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
ax.bar(x - width/2, baseline_coefs, width, label="Baseline", color="#8172B2")
ax.bar(x + width/2, full_coefs, width, label="With controls", color="#4C72B0")
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels([label_map.get(c, c) for c in exposure_cols_model], rotation=20, ha="right")
ax.set_ylabel("Coefficient")
ax.set_title("Task group coefficients, baseline vs. full model")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Nonlinearity

The RESET test rejects the linear specification [TK: statistic and p value], and
@fig-binned shows why. Binned means of affordability salary across the range of routine
cognitive work rise and then fall rather than tracking a straight line.

<!-- FIGURE: fig-binned. EXISTS, poster Figure 5. Binned means of affordability salary
     across the range of routine cognitive, actual and random forest predicted on the same
     axes. Should port over close to as is. The residual plot that pairs with it is
     claimed by _04 as well, resolve before building either. -->

```{python}
#| label: fig-binned
#| fig-cap: "Binned means of affordability salary across routine cognitive employment share, actual vs. Random Forest predicted. The non-monotonic pattern is what a linear model cannot represent."

import matplotlib.ticker as ticker

def binned_means_plot(feature, n_bins=10):
    plot_df = X_test.copy()
    plot_df["actual"] = y_test.values
    plot_df["predicted"] = best_rf.predict(X_test)
    plot_df["bin"] = pd.qcut(plot_df[feature], q=n_bins, duplicates="drop")

    binned = plot_df.groupby("bin", observed=True).agg(
        feature_mean=(feature, "mean"),
        actual_mean=("actual", "mean"),
        predicted_mean=("predicted", "mean"),
    ).reset_index()

    plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 7))
    plt.plot(binned["feature_mean"], binned["actual_mean"], marker="o", label="Actual (binned mean)")
    plt.plot(binned["feature_mean"], binned["predicted_mean"], marker="o", label="RF predicted (binned mean)")
    plt.xlabel(label_map.get(feature, feature))
    plt.ylabel("Affordability Salary ($)")
    plt.title(f"Binned means: {label_map.get(feature, feature)} vs. affordability")
    plt.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.15), ncol=1)
    plt.gca().yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: f"{int(x/1000)}k"))
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.28)
    plt.show()

binned_means_plot("routine_cognitive_share")
```

@fig-modelcomp compares held out performance across specifications. The random forest
reaches a test R² of `{python} f"{results.loc[results['model']=='Random Forest (log target)','test_r2'].values[0]:.3f}"`
against `{python} f"{results.loc[results['model']=='OLS (log target)','test_r2'].values[0]:.3f}"`
for the log-target linear model, and `{python} f"{results.loc[results['model']=='Neural Net','test_r2'].values[0]:.3f}"`
for the neural network. The gap is evidence
that the relationship has curvature the linear model cannot represent, which is the same
conclusion the RESET test reaches by a different route.

     for OLS, ridge, random forest, neural net, showing 0.610, 0.610, 0.840, 0.739.

     which would make it NEW. Decide before building. -->

```{python}
#| label: fig-modelcomp
#| fig-cap: "Held-out test R² across three model specifications. Random Forest and the log-target linear model perform comparably; both outperform the neural net."

display_labels = {
    "OLS (log target)": "Linear Model",
    "Random Forest (log target)": "Random Forest",
    "Neural Net": "Neural Network",
}
chart_labels = results["model"].map(display_labels)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
colors = ["#4C72B0", "#55A868", "#C44E52"]
bars = plt.bar(chart_labels, results["test_r2"], color=colors)
plt.ylabel("Test R²")
plt.title("Model comparison — held-out test R²")
plt.ylim(0, 1)
for bar, val in zip(bars, results["test_r2"]):
    plt.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, val + 0.01, f"{val:.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=20)
plt.xticks(rotation=20, ha="right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## What matters most

Poverty rate is the strongest single feature in the random forest, by a wide margin
(@fig-importance). Task groups follow, with non routine manual ranked highest among them.
This ordering is consistent with the regression: poverty carries most of the explanatory
weight, and the task groups add to it rather than substituting for it.

<!-- FIGURE: fig-importance. EXISTS, poster Figure 6. Feature importance, horizontal
     bars, mean drop in test R squared when shuffled, ordered poverty rate, routine
     cognitive, non routine manual, unemployment, routine manual. Note the poster titles
     it "permutation importance", change to feature importance when porting. -->

```{python}
#| label: fig-importance
#| fig-cap: "Random Forest permutation importance: mean drop in test R² when each feature (or feature group) is shuffled. Poverty rate dominates; task-mix shares follow."

perm_series = pd.Series(perm_imp.importances_mean, index=feature_cols_reg)[core_features].rename(label_map)
perm_series["Year (grouped)"] = year_drop
perm_series["State (grouped)"] = state_drop
perm_series = perm_series.sort_values()

plt.figure(figsize=(5.7, 5))
plt.barh(perm_series.index, perm_series.values, color="#4C72B0")
plt.xlabel("Importance to prediction accuracy")
plt.suptitle("Random Forest permutation importance", fontsize=20, y=0.96)
plt.subplots_adjust(top=0.88, bottom=0.18)
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-importance, permutation importance for
`poverty_rate` at 0.625 is overwhelmingly the
largest number here, which is consistent with every model's findings so far.
`non_routine_manual_share` is the highest of our task-mix categories, with
`routine_manual_share` next, and `routine_cognitive_share` last.

## Stability over time

A county's task mix moves very little across the fifteen year panel [TK: quantify]. This
matters for interpretation. Because the mix is close to a fixed characteristic of place,
the affordability differences associated with it do not fade, and they are not something
residents can be expected to move out from under.
